whatItDoes: Compares the net cost of buying a home versus renting a comparable property over a time horizon. It models the down payment, mortgage payments, property tax, maintenance, home appreciation, and the return the down payment could earn if invested instead.
whyItExists: Whether buying or renting is cheaper depends on how long you stay, prices, rates, and growth projections. A side-by-side net cost shows the real difference instead of the emotional one.
whoShouldUse: Renters considering a first purchase, movers deciding whether to sell and rent, and anyone comparing housing options over a known time horizon.
useCases: Compare buying vs. renting for a 5-year stay
See how long you must stay for buying to win
Test the impact of mortgage rate and appreciation assumptions
Understand the opportunity cost of the down payment
instructions: Enter the home price and the rent of a comparable place
Enter your planned down payment percent and mortgage rate
Set the number of years you plan to stay
Read the verdict and the net cost of each path
examples: $400,000 home vs. $2,000 rent, 20% down, 6.5% rate, 5 years
$300,000 home vs. $1,500 rent, 10% down, 7% rate, 3 years
bestPractices: Use a rent for a home comparable in size and area
Pick a horizon you'll realistically honor
Adjust appreciation and the alternative investment return honestly
Re-run the comparison when rates or prices move
commonMistakes: Comparing rent to mortgage alone and ignoring taxes and maintenance
Forgetting the down payment could have been invested
Assuming appreciation continues at the current pace forever
faq: Why does renting invest the down payment? — Money not tied up in a home is assumed to earn the investment return instead.
Are closing and moving costs included? — No, this simplified version omits them.
What if my horizon is very short? — Short horizons usually favor renting because buying costs are spread thinly.
Is this financial advice? — No, it is a comparison estimate with stated assumptions.
